doc.title: Tom Lellis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 31, 2007

chapter: Advice for singers and life on the road
title: Advice to singers: be the time, shake an egg, know the changes
summary: He tells aspiring singers to become musicians and internalize time, using a shaker egg, and to earn the band's respect.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: What do you say to aspiring jazz musicians these days?
Musicians or singers?
Well don’t you want a singer to be a musician?
Well that’s what I tell them.
Okay.

That’s why I’m delineating. Because there are two things. I don’t have that much influence or run across that many jazz musicians that I can influence. So the singers are the ones that I run into. And I tell them that they will never reach the place that they aspire to unless (a) they become a musician; (b) they are the time, the rhythm. They have
to be the time. They cannot rely on the musicians to take them through the time. They have to reflect it.
That’s great advice. Do you have specific —
Methodologies? Yeah. I make ‘em play shaker.
All right.

I take out, I get a little egg, a two dollar egg, that’s the first thing I say, let’s go buy an egg and then you go play with the radio and rock & roll and funk and R&B and jazz and Latin music and anything you can, obviously straight ahead four-four it’s not the greatest thing, but it doesn’t matter. If they go to the other idioms and get, just, and I tell them you know it’s hard until it’s not. And that might be a day, it might be a month. But it’s hard to do until it’s not and then you lock it in and it becomes that heartbeat and you internalize it and all of a sudden you can conduct with that little egg.
That is great advice.
Thank you.
I’m going to steal that for sure.
Please do.
I’ve got instrumentalists who could profit from that. I just never really thought of that, that it’s obviously that they’re not really internalizing.

Right. I tell them to become part of the rhythm section that way. And when the drummer is playing a solo or if it’s a Latin, a bossa nova, and I tell them, you know, you can conduct. If you’re playing a boss nova and you’re going, and you go, it’s all of a sudden it’s a samba. You can double it up and you can conduct the band that you’re playing with. And it’s an integral part of you immersing yourself into the band and the band knows it. If you have time, the band is going to respect you. It’s not going to be like oh we’ve got to play for the singer. And you know there’s that.
There is.

And we were talking about that, you know you broached that earlier, that there is a definite separation. And some musicians don’t like you because you sing the head. Some musicians don’t like you because they don’t think you’re as talented as they are musically because you’re not a musician. So the burden of a singer is to get through those elements that are holding you down. You have to prove to them that you belong there, number one, and the best way to do that, I have found, is with time and to become — at least know the changes, you know, know the changes. I’ve been on bandstands and I call a tune and the bass player doesn’t know the tune and I’m feeding him the changes and they’re going, “Really?” They don’t believe it. And all of a sudden you have the respect and they play for you so much better.

That’s right. The fellow Rick Montalbano I mentioned, told me a singer joke, it was real though. You know. Someone wanted to sing a tune with him and he said — I have to get this right — he said, “That’s a little high can you do it in minor?”
Oh, no. Right.
You know, that kind of thing.

Yeah, yeah. I believe, that’s right. Well that’s the kind of stuff that, and you know I must come down on a lot of singers that rely on the musicians. There are a lot of singers there that they think they can get away with that. And I tell them all the time it’s your fault, it’s not their fault, it’s the singer’s fault. Your responsibility is to come up to the players, not the players to come down to you. That’s not the ideal.
Wow. Are they teaching that at the New School?
I don’t frankly know. I don’t know. I hope so, but I’m not sure.
